  "title": "TemporalProbe: Which Internal Signal Best Detects Hallucination Onset? A Controlled Comparison of Attention Sinks, Hidden States, and Log-Probabilities as Temporal Features",
  "core_problem": "Multiple internal LLM signals — attention sink scores, hidden-state spectral features, and log-probabilities — have each been independently shown to be effective for hallucination detection when modeled temporally (SinkProbe achieves 23/28 model-dataset wins with static attention sinks; EigenTrack reaches 0.82–0.94 AUROC with GRU-based hidden-state tracking; HALT detects hallucination via GRU on log-probability time series; HSAD gains >10 AUROC points via FFT on cross-layer hidden signals). Yet these results are incomparable: each method uses different architectures, training data, evaluation protocols, and model-benchmark combinations. HALUPROBE (arXiv 2502.13490) partially addressed this gap by systematically comparing attention weights, hidden-state activations, and logits for hallucination detection across three inference stages, finding that 'attention-based features provide more consistent performance across datasets.' Concurrently, Proxy Analyzers (arXiv 2605.07209) compared 18 internal features across 7 analyzer architectures and found that attention-based signals (per-head source-document attention and attention entropy) account for over 88% of Random Forest feature importance — reinforcing HALUPROBE's conclusion that attention signals dominate. However, both comparisons are entirely static: HALUPROBE applies fixed classifiers to per-instance feature snapshots on only two 7B models (Llama-2-7B, Vicuna-7B), and Proxy Analyzers reads already-generated text through a separate proxy model's single forward pass rather than tracking the generating model's own dynamics during generation. Moreover, HALUPROBE's finding is contested by subsequent work showing FFN activations outperform attention features. More fundamentally, static comparison cannot answer three critical questions that require temporal modeling: (1) which signal enables the earliest detection of hallucination during generation (early-detection curves at partial observation), (2) which signal shows the first distributional shift at hallucination onset (temporal lead/lag analysis), and (3) whether the static ranking (attention > hidden states > logits per HALUPROBE; attention dominates per Proxy Analyzers) holds or reverses when signals are modeled as evolving sequences across generation steps. No systematic comparison exists that isolates the signal modality as the independent variable within a temporal framework — training identical temporal classifiers on parallel feature streams extracted from the same generations under the same evaluation protocol. This gap has practical consequences: practitioners building real-time hallucination guardrails must choose a signal type with no principled basis for the choice, and the conflicting static evidence cannot be resolved without temporal analysis that reveals when and how each signal becomes informative during generation.",
  "opportunity": "Four independent research threads have converged to make this temporal comparison both possible and timely. (1) Feature identification: SinkProbe (arXiv 2604.10697) established attention sink scores as the strongest attention-based hallucination signal via logistic regression on per-head sink features, using ℓ₁ regularization in its interpretability analysis (Section 4.1) to identify the most informative head-layer combinations. (2) Temporal architecture: EigenTrack (arXiv 2509.15735) and HALT (arXiv 2602.02888) independently proved that lightweight GRU classifiers on per-step internal features achieve strong hallucination detection — but on hidden-state spectral features and log-probabilities respectively, never on attention patterns. (3) Causal grounding: SinkTrack (ICLR 2026) demonstrated that modifying attention sinks causally affects hallucination rates, and FACTUM (arXiv 2601.05866) showed that correct vs. hallucinated citations differ specifically in attention sink usage patterns — establishing that sinks carry independent hallucination-relevant information, not merely downstream reflections of hidden-state dynamics. (4) Static signal comparison: HALUPROBE (arXiv 2502.13490) and Proxy Analyzers (arXiv 2605.07209) both found attention-based signals dominant in static comparison — HALUPROBE via direct model probing on two 7B models, Proxy Analyzers via 18-feature Random Forest importance across seven analyzer architectures — but neither employed temporal modeling during generation.

The key insight: these threads define a natural factorial experiment. Both static comparisons agree that attention features win in snapshot analysis; we test whether this ranking holds when signals are modeled as temporal sequences during generation. This test is motivated by a principled theoretical hypothesis: attention, hidden states, and log-probabilities occupy different positions in the transformer's computational pipeline and may therefore shift on different timescales during hallucination onset (see Theoretical Motivation below). We have three validated signal types (attention sinks, hidden states, log-probs), one validated temporal architecture (GRU), and shared evaluation infrastructure. By training identical GRU classifiers on parallel feature streams extracted from the same model generations, we can isolate the signal modality as the sole independent variable. This controlled temporal comparison — the first of its kind — is the primary contribution. Three outcomes are possible and all are informative: (a) the static ranking holds temporally, validating HALUPROBE's and Proxy Analyzers' conclusion for real-time deployment; (b) the ranking reverses, revealing that temporal dynamics carry different information than static snapshots; (c) the ranking is task/model-dependent, explaining the contradictory findings across static studies. As part of this comparison, we introduce SinkWatch-GRU, the attention-sink arm that fills the untested cell: a GRU temporal detector consuming per-step attention sink features from SinkProbe's informative heads.",
  "landscape": "**Signal-type comparison for hallucination detection (static):** HALUPROBE (arXiv 2502.13490, Feb 2025) is the most directly related prior work: it systematically compares attention weights, hidden-state activations (FFN outputs), and logits for hallucination detection across three inference stages (understanding/query/generation) on Llama-2-7B and Vicuna-7B, using HaluEval and CNNDM. Key finding: attention-based lookback ratio achieves highest accuracy (0.75 HaluEval, 0.83 CNNDM), with attention entropy showing robust discrimination. However, HALUPROBE has critical limitations: (a) only static classifiers, no temporal modeling; (b) only two older 7B models; (c) limited transferability — CNNDM-trained models achieve ~0.50 on HaluEval; (d) zero venue publications or citations; (e) the finding is contested — a subsequent empirical study (krogoldAI, HuggingFace Dec 2025) found FFN activations (82.96% accuracy, 91.04% AUC) outperform attention statistics (79.90%, 88.46% AUC), concluding attention 'added no value beyond what FFN activations already provided.' Proxy Analyzers (arXiv 2605.07209, May 2026) introduces a complementary static comparison: it reads already-generated text through a small open-weight proxy model (0.5B–9B parameters across seven architectures: Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia, LLaMA-3) and detects hallucinations from the proxy's internal activations across 18 features (residual norms, per-head attention, entropy, MLP activations, logit-lens trajectories, token-level grounding statistics). Using Random Forest feature importance, they find that per-head source-document attention and attention entropy together account for over 88% of importance across all seven models — reinforcing HALUPROBE's attention-dominance conclusion from an independent methodology. However, Proxy Analyzers operates post-hoc on a separate proxy model rather than the generating model, and does not employ temporal modeling during generation. TemporalProbe differs fundamentally from both: it compares features from the generating model's own temporal dynamics during autoregressive generation, not from static snapshots or proxy-model forward passes. UniFact (arXiv 2512.02772, Dec 2025) provides a unified evaluation framework comparing hallucination detection (internal signals) vs. fact verification (external knowledge), benchmarking SAPLMA (hidden states), MIND (final-layer embeddings), and logit-based methods — but does not compare attention patterns, does not analyze layer-wise signals, and treats detection as single-shot classification without temporal modeling. **No prior work compares signal types under temporal modeling during generation.**

**Attention-based hallucination detection (static):** SinkProbe (arXiv 2604.10697, April 2026) proved sink scores outperform spectral Laplacian eigenvalues in 23/28 model-dataset pairs via logistic regression on attention sink features (AUROC 0.778 on TruthfulQA, 0.890 on HaluEval-QA for Llama-3.1-8B), with ℓ₁-regularized variant used for interpretability to identify informative heads. LapEigvals (EMNLP 2025, arXiv 2502.17598) established spectral attention features as hallucination signals. CHARM (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2509.24770) applies GNNs on attributed attention graphs combining attention and activation features. Spectral Guardrails (arXiv 2602.08082, Feb 2026) achieves 97.7% recall via training-free spectral attention topology analysis. AggTruth (ICCS 2025, arXiv 2506.18628) aggregates attention scores with windowing. TOHA (ACL 2026, arXiv 2504.10063) uses topological divergence on attention graphs. Frequency-Aware Attention (arXiv 2602.18145) shows high-frequency attention energy correlates with hallucination. FACTUM (arXiv 2601.05866) uses attention sink usage as one of four mechanistic signals. **All compute features from static snapshots; none model attention feature trajectories across generation steps.**

**Temporal/trajectory hallucination analysis:** Hallucination as Trajectory Commitment (arXiv 2604.15400, April 2026) provides causal evidence that residual-stream trajectories bifurcate at the first generated token in 44.3% of prompts on Qwen2.5-1.5B, with asymmetric attractor dynamics — but tested only residual-stream activations on a single small model, not attention patterns. Before the First Token (arXiv 2604.13068) demonstrates scale-dependent emergence of hallucination signals at position zero. Hallucination Basins (arXiv 2604.04743) formalizes hallucination as trajectory capture in latent-space basins. HalluSAE (arXiv 2604.16430) models hallucination as phase transitions in latent dynamics via sparse autoencoders. Attractor Geometry (arXiv 2605.05686, May 2026) models facts as attractor basins in hidden-state space. First Hallucination Tokens (arXiv 2507.20836) shows the first hallucinated token is far more detectable. Shadows in the Attention (arXiv 2505.16894) reveals an 'attention-locking' threshold (JS-Drift ~0.69) — but tracks drift across prompt perturbation rounds, not generation steps. Step-Level Hallucination Detection via Hidden-State Transport Geometry (arXiv 2605.13772, May 2026) frames hallucination as localized excursion in transport cost along hidden-state trajectories, using BiLSTM on geometric transition features — exclusively on hidden states, not attention. **All study residual-stream or mixed-modality dynamics; none systematically compare signal modalities under controlled conditions.**

**Temporal feature tracking for detection (methods):** EigenTrack (arXiv 2509.15735, 2025) tracks temporal spectral dynamics of hidden-state covariance via GRU (0.82–0.94 AUROC). HALT (arXiv 2602.02888, Feb 2026) treats log-probs as time series via bidirectional GRU (hidden_dim=256, 5 layers). HSAD (arXiv 2509.13154, Sep 2025) applies FFT to cross-layer hidden-state activations, achieving 82.5% AUROC on TruthfulQA and 92.1% on TriviaQA for Qwen-2.5-7B — conceptually related but models vertical dynamics (across layers within a single step) rather than horizontal dynamics (across generation steps). TDGNet (arXiv 2602.08048) targets diffusion language models only. ICR Probe (ACL 2025, arXiv 2507.16488) tracks cross-layer hidden-state evolution (0.73–0.84 AUROC). **Each validates temporal modeling for one signal type but no paper compares signal types under identical temporal architectures.**

**Real-time/online detection:** MIND (ACL Findings 2024, arXiv 2403.06448) is the foundational real-time internal-state detector: an unsupervised framework using last-layer contextualized embeddings with an MLP, achieving passage-level AUC 0.89–0.96 with only 3.3% overhead — but operates post-generation on the final hidden state, uses no temporal modeling, and does not leverage attention patterns. PCNet/PC-LDCD (arXiv 2605.05953, May 2026) trains probabilistic circuits on hidden-state residual stream for online detection; on TruthfulQA specifically, PCNet achieves 0.66–0.81 AUROC across models (0.75±0.06 for Llama-3.1-8B), substantially lower than its 0.95–0.98 AUROC on CoQA/SQuAD — highlighting that TruthfulQA poses a harder detection challenge where improved methods are most needed. RAUQ (arXiv 2505.20045) identifies 'uncertainty-aware' attention heads and recurrently aggregates weights for sequence-level uncertainty — uses simple aggregation (not learned temporal model), targets generic attention (not sinks), operates at sequence granularity. DRIFT (arXiv 2601.14210) trains lightweight probes on hidden states (<0.1% overhead, SOTA on 10/12 settings). Real-Time Entity Detection (arXiv 2509.03531) achieves AUC 0.90 via linear probes on hidden states. Streaming Hallucination Detection (arXiv 2601.02170) treats step-level hallucination as evolving latent state. Monitoring Decoding (ACL Findings 2025, arXiv 2503.03106) uses external reference model logits with 5.7× overhead. **All use hidden-state, logit, or generic attention features; none apply learned temporal models to attention sink features, and none compare signal modalities.**

**Attention sink context:** Attention Sink Survey (arXiv 2604.10098) reviews 180+ papers. SinkTrack (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2604.10027) converts passive attention sinks into active context anchors — demonstrating causal relevance. TARAC (arXiv 2504.04099) tracks visual attention decay in VLMs for mitigation. Mirage in the Eyes (USENIX Security 2025, arXiv 2501.15269) exploits sinks for adversarial attacks.

**The open gap:** (1) Both static comparisons (HALUPROBE and Proxy Analyzers) agree that attention-based features dominate for hallucination detection in snapshot analysis, but neither uses temporal modeling — meaning the field cannot determine which signal is earliest to detect hallucination during generation, whether the static ranking holds temporally, or whether signals carry complementary temporal information. (2) No method applies learned temporal modeling to attention sink features during autoregressive text generation.",
  "approach": "We propose TemporalProbe, a controlled experimental framework for comparing which internal temporal signal — attention sinks, hidden-state spectral features, or log-probabilities — is most informative for detecting hallucination during autoregressive generation. The framework trains identical GRU classifiers on parallel feature streams extracted from the same model generations, isolating the signal modality as the independent variable. We explicitly position this as the temporal extension of HALUPROBE's and Proxy Analyzers' static comparisons: both found attention features dominant statically; we test whether this ranking holds, reverses, or becomes task-dependent when signals are modeled as temporal sequences during generation. As part of this comparison, we introduce SinkWatch-GRU, the first learned temporal detector on attention sink features, filling the untested cell in the comparison.

**Theoretical Motivation: Why Temporal Ranking May Differ from Static Ranking.** The three signal types occupy fundamentally different positions in the transformer's computational pipeline, corresponding to different functional roles established by mechanistic interpretability research. Attention heads function as information routing mechanisms — they determine WHERE the model reads from its context, with specialized retrieval heads identified as the primary contributors to long-context information access (Wu et al., ICLR 2025). Hidden states (residual-stream activations) represent the accumulated result of WHAT the model has computed — the running tally of transformations across layers, where FFN sublayers function as key-value memories storing and retrieving factual knowledge (Geva et al., EMNLP 2021). Log-probabilities reflect the model's output confidence — HOW certain it is about the next token, a downstream consequence of both routing and computation. Because routing decisions (attention) causally precede the computation they gate (hidden-state updates via FFN), and both precede the final output distribution (log-probs), these signals may shift on different timescales during hallucination onset: a routing error — attending to irrelevant context or failing to retrieve the right source passage — may manifest in attention features before the residual stream fully incorporates the erroneous information, and well before the output distribution reflects reduced confidence. This creates a testable prediction: attention-based signals should be leading indicators that shift earliest, hidden-state features should be concurrent indicators reflecting the computation going awry, and log-probability features should be lagging indicators that shift only once the erroneous computation propagates to the output. The temporal lead/lag analysis in our framework directly tests this hypothesis. If confirmed, it explains why static comparisons (which collapse temporal order) find attention dominant — attention features encode the earliest, most informative signal. If refuted (e.g., log-probs shift first because confidence calibration is more sensitive than routing patterns), this would reveal that the transformer's computational pipeline does not produce hallucination signals in the expected causal order, a finding with implications for mechanistic interpretability beyond hallucination detection.

**What Temporal Comparison Uniquely Reveals Beyond Static Comparison.** Three analyses are impossible with static classifiers and constitute our primary novel contributions over HALUPROBE and Proxy Analyzers: (1) Early-detection curves: AUROC as a function of the fraction of the response observed (at 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of tokens) — revealing which signal enables detection earliest, critical for real-time guardrails. (2) Temporal lead/lag analysis: measuring when each signal first shows significant distributional shift relative to annotated hallucination onset — determining whether attention sinks, hidden states, or log-probs are leading or lagging indicators, directly testing the theoretical prediction above. (3) Complementarity dynamics: whether signals that are redundant in static snapshots carry orthogonal information when modeled temporally (e.g., attention sinks may drift gradually while log-probs shift abruptly, providing complementary temporal signatures).

**Experimental Framework: Three Parallel Arms with Controlled Architecture.** For each generation, we extract three parallel feature streams at every decoding step t:

*Arm 1 — SinkWatch (Attention Sinks):* Per-step features from the top-K informative head-layer combinations (K=5–15) identified via SinkProbe's ℓ₁-regularized interpretability analysis: (a) sink scores for top-k sink tokens (k=2–3), (b) sink concentration (max sink / total sink), (c) sink entropy, (d) context-attention ratio. Augmented with first-order temporal derivatives. Raw dimensionality ~50–120.

*Arm 2 — EigenTrack-style (Hidden States):* Per-step spectral features from sliding-window covariance matrices of hidden-state activations: leading eigenvalues, spectral gaps, entropy, and RMT statistics. Matching EigenTrack's feature design. Raw dimensionality ~10–20.

*Arm 3 — HALT-style (Log-Probabilities):* Per-step log-probability features: token log-prob, predictive entropy, top-k probability gap, rank. Matching HALT's feature design. Raw dimensionality ~25.

**Handling Feature Dimensionality Differences Across Arms.** The three arms have substantially different raw feature dimensionalities (~50–120 for SinkWatch, ~10–20 for EigenTrack-style, ~25 for HALT-style). To ensure a truly controlled comparison, each arm includes a per-arm learned linear projection layer that maps its raw features to a common dimension d=32 before feeding into the GRU. This design ensures the GRU itself is architecturally identical across all three arms (same hidden_dim, same number of parameters in the recurrent layers), isolating the information content of the input signal rather than confounding the comparison with differences in input dimensionality or parameter count. The per-arm projection layers are the only components that differ, and their parameter counts are negligible relative to the GRU (~2K–4K vs. ~25K parameters).

All three streams feed into identical unidirectional GRUs (hidden_dim=64, ~25K recurrent parameters each), trained with identical binary cross-entropy loss, hyperparameters, and data splits. This controlled design isolates the feature modality — same temporal architecture, same training data, same evaluation.

**Important Note on Architecture Choice.** Our comparison GRUs (unidirectional, ~25K recurrent parameters, hidden_dim=64) are deliberately much smaller than the architectures used in the original papers: HALT uses a 5-layer bidirectional GRU with hidden_dim=256 (~5M parameters), and EigenTrack uses a different GRU configuration. This is the correct design choice for controlled comparison — using identical, lightweight architectures isolates the signal modality as the independent variable. However, this means absolute AUROC numbers for each arm should NOT be compared against the original papers' reported numbers, which benefit from architectures specifically tuned for each signal type. The value of our comparison lies in the RELATIVE ranking across arms under identical architecture, not in absolute performance.

**Primary Analysis: Cross-Signal Comparison.** (1) Detection performance: AUROC and AUPRC for each signal arm at sequence level. (2) Early-detection curves: AUROC as a function of the fraction of the response observed (at 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of tokens), testing which signal enables earliest detection. (3) Temporal lead/lag analysis: measuring when each signal first shows significant distributional shift relative to annotated hallucination onset, directly testing the theoretical prediction that attention signals are leading indicators. (4) Complementarity: late-fusion ensemble combining all three streams to test whether signals carry redundant or orthogonal information; mutual information analysis between per-step predictions from each arm. (5) Static-vs-temporal ranking comparison: explicitly comparing the signal ranking from our temporal GRUs against HALUPROBE's static ranking, Proxy Analyzers' feature importance ranking, and against static logistic regression baselines on the same features, to test whether temporal modeling changes the winner. (6) Ablation: SinkWatch-GRU vs. SinkWatch-LR (logistic regression on windowed features) to quantify the benefit of learned temporal modeling over simple aggregation.

**Statistical Rigor: Confidence Intervals and Variance Control.** With 1K examples and 25K-parameter GRU models, small-sample variance is a concern. We address this with: (1) 5-fold stratified cross-validation as the primary evaluation protocol, reporting mean and standard deviation across folds for all metrics (AUROC, AUPRC, early-detection curves). (2) Bootstrap confidence intervals (1000 resamples) on the test-fold predictions to provide 95% CIs for all pairwise comparisons between arms. (3) Paired permutation tests (10,000 permutations) to assess whether observed differences between arms are statistically significant (p < 0.05). (4) We report effect sizes (Cohen's d) alongside p-values to distinguish statistically significant from practically meaningful differences. This protocol ensures that our cross-signal ranking claims are grounded in statistical evidence rather than point estimates from a single split.

**Temporal Characterization (Supporting Analysis).** Statistical tests (paired t-test, Kolmogorov-Smirnov) on sink feature distributions at and before annotated hallucination onset points for 500 examples with hallucination onset annotation. This provides the first empirical evidence on whether attention sink features exhibit gradual drift (enabling temporal detection) or abrupt bifurcation (matching the Trajectory Commitment paper's finding for residual-stream activations).

**Entity-Match Annotation Limitations and Mitigation.** We acknowledge that TruthfulQA contains many nuanced factual claims (e.g., 'What happens if you swallow gum?') where entity-match onset annotation is unreliable — correct answers involve reasoning about consequences, not entity identification. This limitation affects the temporal lead/lag analysis (which requires token-level onset annotation) but NOT the primary cross-signal comparison (which uses sequence-level NLI labels). We mitigate this in three ways: (1) For the EMNLP short paper, we restrict temporal lead/lag analysis to a curated subset of ~300 TruthfulQA questions with clear entity-based answers (e.g., 'Who invented X?', 'What is the capital of Y?'), reporting coverage and selection criteria. (2) We supplement entity-match with NLI-based sliding-window annotation: an NLI model evaluates each sliding window of generated tokens against the gold reference, and onset is defined as the first window where entailment drops below threshold. (3) We report the agreement rate between entity-match and NLI-window onset annotations on the curated subset to quantify annotation reliability. For the AAAI full paper, we add TriviaQA (where entity matching is more reliable for factoid questions) as the primary benchmark for temporal lead/lag analysis.

**Pilot Design and Explicit Decision Rule (First 48 hours).** Before full-scale experiments, run a 2-hour pilot on 100 TruthfulQA examples with Llama-3.1-8B: extract per-step sink features, plot distributions for factual vs. hallucinated tokens at generation fractions (25/50/75/100%). **Decision rule:** If the pilot shows that sink features bifurcate abruptly at the first generated token (matching arXiv 2604.15400's findings for residual stream in ≥70% of examples), then temporal GRU modeling may offer no advantage over static SinkProbe for the sink arm specifically. In this case, we (a) proceed with the cross-signal comparison as the primary contribution (which remains novel and valuable regardless), (b) report the abrupt-bifurcation finding as an empirical result extending arXiv 2604.15400 from residual-stream to attention-sink signals, and (c) investigate whether hidden-state or log-prob arms still benefit from temporal modeling (creating an informative asymmetry across signal types). The paper's contribution is resilient: even if SinkWatch-GRU ≈ static SinkProbe, the controlled cross-signal temporal comparison and the early-detection curves remain the first of their kind.

**Intervention (Extension, AAAI 2027 only).** When the best-performing arm's running probability exceeds a high-confidence threshold, trigger DoLa contrastive decoding for subsequent tokens. Evaluate hallucination rate reduction.

**Dual-Target Venue Strategy:**

*EMNLP 2026 (ARR May 25 — short paper, 4 pages):* Radically descoped. 1 model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), 1 benchmark (TruthfulQA, matching SinkProbe), 1K examples, entity-match onset annotation on curated subset + NLI sequence-level labels. Focus: cross-signal comparison (3 arms) + SinkWatch-GRU vs. static SinkProbe + early-detection curves + static-vs-temporal ranking comparison against HALUPROBE's and Proxy Analyzers' findings. Key result: which temporal signal is strongest/earliest for hallucination detection, and whether the static ranking holds. 5-fold cross-validation with bootstrap CIs for all claims. No intervention experiments, no 70B model.

*AAAI 2027 (full paper, 8 pages):* Complete framework. 3 models (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Llama-3.1-70B), 3 benchmarks (TruthfulQA, TriviaQA, HaluEval-QA), 2K examples per pair. Full cross-signal comparison, temporal characterization, complementarity analysis, DoLa intervention, temporal lead/lag on TriviaQA (where entity-match is more reliable), comprehensive ablations.

**Training and Evaluation.** Generate outputs, annotate with binary factual/hallucinated labels via NLI against gold references (validated by manual spot-check of 200 examples), evaluated via 5-fold stratified cross-validation. For EMNLP short paper: NLI-based sequence-level annotation + entity-match onset annotation on curated TruthfulQA subset.

**Baselines.** Static: SinkProbe, LapEigvals, TOHA. Temporal: EigenTrack, HALT. Online: MIND (unsupervised hidden-state), DRIFT, RAUQ, PCNet. Static signal comparison: HALUPROBE-style logistic regression on each feature type (our replication). Ablation: SinkWatch-LR.

**Evaluation Metrics.** Primary: AUROC and AUPRC with 95% bootstrap CIs. Secondary: early-detection AUROC at partial observation, F1 at calibrated threshold, latency overhead (ms/token), mutual information between arms, Cohen's d effect sizes for pairwise arm comparisons. For intervention (AAAI only): hallucination rate reduction and fluency preservation.",

Hidden states (residual-stream activations) represent the accumulated result of WHAT the model has computed — the running tally of transformations across layers, where FFN sublayers function as key-value memories storing and retrieving factual knowledge (Geva et al., EMNLP 2021). Log-probabilities reflect the model's output confidence — HOW certain it is about the next token, a downstream consequence of both routing and computation. Because routing decisions (attention) causally precede the computation they gate (hidden-state updates via FFN), and both precede the final output distribution (log-probs), these signals may shift on different timescales during hallucination onset: a routing error — attending to irrelevant context or failing to retrieve the right source passage — may manifest in attention features before the residual stream fully incorporates the erroneous information, and well before the output distribution reflects reduced confidence. This creates a testable prediction: attention-based signals should be leading indicators that shift earliest, hidden-state features should be concurrent indicators reflecting the computation going awry, and log-probability features should be lagging indicators that shift only once the erroneous computation propagates to the output. The temporal lead/lag analysis in our framework directly tests this hypothesis. If confirmed, it explains why static comparisons (which collapse temporal order) find attention dominant — attention features encode the earliest, most informative signal. If refuted (e.g., log-probs shift first because confidence calibration is more sensitive than routing patterns), this would reveal that the transformer's computational pipeline does not produce hallucination signals in the expected causal order, a finding with implications for mechanistic interpretability beyond hallucination detection.

Here are the consolidated findings across all five searches.

---

## 1. FFN Activations vs. Attention for Hallucination Detection

**Found the exact blog post.** [krogoldAI on HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/blog/krogoldAI/llm-hallucination-detection) reports an empirical study using Ministral-8B on 145,169 labeled examples. Key results:

- **FFN hidden-state activations (mean-pooled across response tokens) are sufficient** -- attention features (per-head stats and MHA outputs) added no value beyond what FFN activations already provided.
- Discriminative signal is **concentrated in specific mid-layers** (particularly layer 16); a single layer suffices for detection (84% accuracy, 91% AUC, 75% F1).
- Extraction uses `llmscan`, a lightweight library they released.

**Corroborating work:** LLM-Check (NSF-published) independently found that **hidden-state-based methods (SAPLMA) outperform logits-based and attention-based methods** in most cases, attributing this to denser hidden-state representations retaining more informative signals. Additionally, ICLR 2025 published [REDEEP](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/7daf60e805e596c3bd1e843e72ea5560-Paper-Conference.pdf), which also uses internal representations for detection. A [spectral features of attention maps paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.17598v2) explores attention-based detection but appears to achieve weaker results than hidden-state approaches.

---

## 2. Multi-Signal Fusion for Hallucination Detection

The state of the art is moving toward combining multiple signals, but **no single dominant fusion framework has emerged**:

- **LLM-Check** explicitly compares hidden representations, attention similarity maps, and logit outputs, finding hidden states superior but noting complementarity.
- **LaaB** (Logical Consistency-as-a-Bridge, [May 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.03971v1)) bridges neural features and symbolic self-judgments via a "meta-judgment" process.
- **Uncertainty-Aware Fusion (UAF)** ([ACM WWW 2025](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3701716.3715523)) combines multiple LLMs based on accuracy and self-assessed uncertainty.
- **EDCIM** integrates lightweight open-source LLMs with proprietary models, using a single hyperparameter to control the cost-accuracy tradeoff.
- **OpenReview work on agent tool selection** detects hallucinations from internal representations during the same forward pass -- computationally efficient real-time detection.

---

## 3. Entity-Based Annotation of TruthfulQA / Token-Level Onset Detection

**No work was found that specifically does entity-based re-annotation of TruthfulQA for token-level hallucination onset.** However, closely related work exists:

- **HaluGate** (vLLM blog, [Dec 2025](https://blog.vllm.ai/2025/12/14/halugate.html)) performs token-level hallucination detection using NER-style entity extraction + NLI verification. Their annotation pipeline uses a frontier LLM to extract entities, web-search for corroboration, and label ungrounded entities as hallucinations -- providing token-level labels.
- [**"First Hallucination Tokens Are Different from Conditional Ones"**](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.20836v4) -- directly studies the onset point of hallucination at the token level.
- **ETF** (Entity Tracing Framework, [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.14748)) traces entity hallucinations in code summaries.
- **"Mitigating Entity-Level Hallucination"** ([OpenReview](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=Nx9gXrQQ2n)) addresses entity-level detection specifically.

TruthfulQA itself is used in hallucination benchmarking but appears not to have been re-annotated at the entity/token level for onset detection. This looks like **an open gap**.

---

## 4. Early/Partial-Generation Detection

Several groups have studied detection performance as a function of generation progress:

- **Real-time token-by-token monitoring** frameworks continuously score factuality of the partial response during generation and dynamically alter the decoding trajectory when imminent hallucination is detected, addressing the snowballing effect.
- **Intermediate-layer probes** (3M--37M params) can be trained on hidden states from middle layers, with two modes: question-only (runs before/alongside generation, zero added latency) and question+answer (waits for full response, higher accuracy).
- **HalMit** ([arXiv 2507.15903](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.15903v1)) uses progressive generalization bound exploration with a black-box watchdog monitor for persistent hallucination detection during generation.
- **"Low-Cost Black-Box Detection via Dynamical System Prediction"** ([arXiv 2605.05134](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.05134)) -- a May 2026 paper on cheap detection approaches.

---

## 5. Adaptive Compute / Speculative Detection / Cheap-Signal Gating

**Strong precedent exists in speculative decoding, and it is now being applied to hallucination detection:**

- **Speculative decoding** (now mainstream) uses a small draft model to propose tokens and a large verifier to check them, with 2--3x speedups. The key idea of **using cheap signals to gate expensive computation** is well-established.
- **Energy-efficient speculative decoding** ([arXiv 2508.12590](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.12590v1)) filters tokens for verification using two lightweight signals: (i) epistemic uncertainty from temperature perturbations and (ii) token importance from attention-weight statistics. A token is uploaded for expensive verification **only when it is both uncertain and important**.
- **HaluGate** implements exactly a cost-gating architecture: a lightweight Sentinel classifier first determines whether a query even warrants fact-checking (72.2% of queries skipped for creative/code tasks), then runs detection only when needed (~125ms for 4K context).
- **Collective and Adaptive Speculative Decoding** ([ACM SC25](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3712285.3759834)) dynamically adjusts speculation length based on runtime acceptance rates.

---

## Your Specific Questions

**Is there work exploiting different computational costs of attention vs. hidden-state vs. logit features?**

Partially. LLM-Check explicitly compares these three signal types and reports up to 45x and 450x speedups over baselines, and the krogoldAI work shows a single mid-layer FFN extraction suffices (minimizing overhead). However, **no paper was found that explicitly builds a cascading/tiered system** that first checks cheap logit entropy, then escalates to hidden-state probes, then to full attention analysis based on a cost-accuracy tradeoff. The closest precedent is the speculative decoding paradigm (cheap draft -> expensive verify) and HaluGate's sentinel pre-classifier (cheap routing -> expensive detection). This tiered-cost architecture for internal hallucination signals appears to be **an open research direction**.

**Has anyone studied the compute-accuracy tradeoff in real-time hallucination monitoring?**

Yes, but mostly in terms of **method-level comparisons** (hidden states vs. logits vs. attention vs. LLM-as-judge) rather than as a systematic Pareto frontier. LLM-Check provides the most explicit cost comparison (45x--450x speedup figures). EDCIM provides a tunable cost-accuracy dial via a single hyperparameter. HaluGate provides latency numbers (125ms--365ms). But a **systematic study of the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier across all internal signal types at varying generation fractions** does not appear to exist yet.
